title: E2E latency variance by sequence-length and cold-start behavior
content:
Executive summary:

This note captures profiling results and hypotheses from an e2e trace sweep focused on two axes: request sequence length (64 vs 512 tokens) and cold-start effects (cold worker, warm worker, and cached-KV state). Goal: identify dominant contributors to p95/p99 tail and actionable mitigations that fit our production constraints (no model changes, prefer runtime/ops fixes).

Key findings (short):
- p50 is dominated by GPU compute for long sequences, but p95/p99 tail is dominated by intermittent host-side stalls (cold allocator, memcpy spikes, and per-request KV load contention).
- Cold-starts (worker spin-up + allocator priming) add a median ~30–80ms overhead depending on model size, pushing many p95s over SLO for low-latency tiers.
- Sequence-length scaling is near-linear for compute p50, but tail amplification (p99) grows superlinearly due to batching edge cases and memory thrash when token KB cache is populated mid-request.
- Network serialization + TLS renegotiation accounted for ~10–15% of observed tail in a subset of traces from older front-door proxies.

Workloads & dataset: 
- Synthetic request generator used to produce 10k traces per cell, per scenario (64-token and 512-token prompt lengths), mixed with production-like arrival patterns (Poisson λ tuned to 65% utilization).
- Traces collected with distributed tracing enabled (span tags: route, model_variant, tenant_tier, seq_len, batch_size). Sampling was stratified: 100% of p99 candidates and 5% of p50 population to ensure tail fidelity.

Span definitions (what we measure):
- client -> frontdoor: network RTT and front-door processing (TLS, auth)
- router -> queue: routing and prequeue work (rate-limit checks)
- queue: time spent waiting to be picked by a worker slot
- worker-setup: cold worker init (cuda context, allocator warm-up, loading micro-kernels)
- request-parse: payload parsing and tokenization on host
- kv-load: loading prefix KV cache from shared memory or file-backed cache
- gpu-exec: end-to-end on-GPU time (attention, matmuls, softmax, kv-cache lookups inside kernels)
- gpu-post: gather outputs, dequantize, logits-to-tokens on CPU if present
- emit: network send back to client

Representative aggregated metrics (median / p95 / p99) for scenario A: 64-token, warm workers, 65% util:
- e2e total: p50=28ms, p95=105ms, p99=230ms
- queue: p50=0.6ms, p95=6ms, p99=24ms
- worker-setup: p50=0.0ms, p95=0.0ms, p99=0.0ms (warm)
- request-parse: p50=1.1ms, p95=3.8ms, p99=9.6ms
- kv-load: p50=0.7ms, p95=12ms, p99=54ms (rare remote fetches)
- gpu-exec: p50=18ms, p95=70ms, p99=128ms
- gpu-post: p50=1.2ms, p95=3.6ms, p99=9.0ms
- emit: p50=1.4ms, p95=4.1ms, p99=12ms

Scenario B: 512-token, warm workers, same util:
- e2e total: p50=110ms, p95=320ms, p99=760ms
- queue: p50=1.8ms, p95=10ms, p99=56ms
- kv-load: p50=4.2ms, p95=48ms, p99=210ms (KV cache population steps visible)
- gpu-exec: p50=84ms, p95=250ms, p99=520ms

Cold-start scenario (64 token, half requests hit cold worker due to autoscale or eviction):
- cold worker-setup: median 48ms, p95 190ms, p99 420ms (includes CUDA context, allocator warm-up, kernel JIT in some cases)
- e2e total with 50% cold mix: p50=44ms, p95=180ms, p99=460ms

Observations & trace archetypes: 
1) KV-cache miss storms: When many requests for long prefixes arrive to a newly started worker, kv-loads cause synchronous file/shm reads that serialize and appear as 40–200ms spikes (all recorded in kv-load span). Mitigation: async prefetch or background hot page population and read-ahead policy.

2) Allocator fragmentation / slow host memcpy: p99 traces repeatedly show a host memcpy span that grows to hundreds of ms when host-side memory is fragmented (observed after sustained high allocation churn from batched requests with variable sequence lengths). Mitigation: pool allocator tuning; use pinned memory pools; reuse buffers per-worker.

3) GPU micro-kernel JIT/first-run spikes: Certain custom CUDA kernels (sparsity, fused-attention) show first-invocation cost on new worker (JIT + kernel load) — these are visible in worker-setup or early gpu-exec spans. Mitigation: pre-warm kernels during worker start or use precompiled kernels.

4) Batcher edge-cases: Under our autoscale policy, single-request batches at tail get processed with full per-batch overhead; p99 often has single large batch with expensive enqueue/dequeue locking. Mitigation: adaptive micro-batching thresholds and fast-path for size-1.

5) Network front-door TLS renegotiation: ~10% of tail traces show a spike in client->frontdoor due to long-lived TLS session teardown on edge proxies (older versions). Fixing proxy config reduced this in canary.

Trace example (single p99 waterfall snippet, 2026-03-07, trace id ab12ef78):
- client->frontdoor: 18ms (TLS renegotiate 14ms)
- router->queue: 2ms
- queue: 42ms
- worker-setup: 0ms
- request-parse: 2.8ms
- kv-load: 172ms (blocked on file-backed page reads)
- gpu-exec: 98ms
- gpu-post: 5.4ms
- emit: 5.6ms
- total: 347.8ms

Hypotheses prioritized: 
- H1: KV-cache misses dominate p99 for medium-to-long inputs. Priority: high. Action: server-side async prefetch and increase shared shm resident set for top-100 prefixes. (SERV-278)
- H2: Host allocator churn causes memcpy/p99 spikes. Priority: high. Action: implement per-worker pinned buffer pools + limit ephemeral allocations in tokenizer paths (PR #891).
- H3: Cold worker JIT overheads cause tail during rapid autoscale. Priority: medium. Action: pre-initialize CUDA contexts and pre-touch kernels during scale-up path.

Immediate action items (next 2 weeks):
- Short-term (engineers): add histogram-based live metric for kv-load latency by tenant and seq_len; add a traced counter for 'kv-cache-miss' per-request. Owner: Luca. Due: 2026-03-18.
- Short-term (infra): enable pinned memory pool feature flag on canary cluster and run 48-hour soak. Owner: Priya. Due: 2026-03-20.
- Medium-term (runtime): implement async KV prefetch and background page-population for worker hot-path. Owner: Jonah. Dep: perf and infra, target 2026-04-08.
- Ops: rotate front-door proxies to newer TLS config across EU region; validate tail reduction. Owner: ops-team. Due: 2026-03-16.

Open questions / follow-ups: 
- What percentage of tenants trigger kv-cache miss storms vs single-tenant noisy neighbors? Need tenant correlation (use linked SERV tickets).
- Are memcpy spikes correlated with particular batch-size patterns (mixed seq_len)? Collect a gated trace with seq_len-tagged batching.
- Can we move to precompiled kernels for top-3 model variants without blocking model onboarding?

Notes on sampling bias and confidence:
- We oversampled p99 candidates to ensure tail fidelity; however, routing-level stochasticity (multi-region fallback) can create nonstationary behavior — plan to run 72h continuous sweep across regions and apply stratified sampling by tenant-tier.

Appendix: quick checklist for reproducing a p99 kv-load spike locally:
1) Start a worker with empty shm KV population (simulate cold worker).
2) Fire 200 concurrent 512-token requests with overlapping prefixes that require disk-backed pages.
3) Observe kv-load span on host growing to 100–300ms.
4) Re-run with pinned memory pools enabled; expect reduction in host memcpy duration.

If you want a narrower drill (per-tenant breakdown, or full trace dumps for top 20 p99 traces), reply with which slice (tenant, region, model) and I'll attach raw trace CSVs and flamegraphs.

-- Samira
